financial_checks.claim: A vehicle was stolen every 5 minutes in the UK in 2024
financial_checks.result: Thatcham Research/NaVCIS (June 2025) reports a vehicle stolen every five minutes in 2024; other outlets report four minutes. Holds. (from search snippets; not independently confirmed)

financial_checks.claim: Seized stolen vehicles 2021-2024: nearly 40% to the Democratic Republic of Congo, 20% to the UAE, then Cyprus, Jamaica, Georgia
financial_checks.result: NaVCIS: DRC 38.5%, UAE 20.1%, Cyprus 6.7%, Jamaica 5.7%, Georgia 5.1% (seizure-based). Holds. (from search snippets; not independently confirmed)

financial_checks.claim: About 70,000 phones stolen in London in 2024, "up by more than 30%"; Britain accounts for 40% of phones stolen in Europe; three quarters of UK phone thefts are in London
financial_checks.result: Met data summarised in news: about 81,365-81,439 in 2024 (up about 36%), then about 71,391 in 2025 (down 12%). One source gives 40% as a gang's share of London phone theft; the Europe-wide 40% and the three-quarters London share (attributed to the Met Police in the narration) were not located. (from search snippets; not independently confirmed)

financial_checks.claim: Hilux £40,000, thief paid £1,500; Range Rover Sport £80,000 to £120,000+ in the UAE; 25 days to Jebel Ali; Border Force inspects under 2% of outbound freight; over 77% of car thefts unsolved; prosecutions halved in a decade
financial_checks.result: Not verified; the narration attributes only the "three quarters of phone thefts are in London" claim to the Met Police; the other statistics carry no attribution in the video.

financial_checks.claim: Time reference "flooding in the UAE ... in April last year"
financial_checks.result: Dubai flooding was April 2024; "last year" is correct for a 2025 script but the registry publication date is 2026-08-13, so the phrase is stale.

strengths: Strong image-led hook and a clear end-to-end pipeline explanation.
Key vehicle statistics are accurate and correctly framed as seizure data.
Plain-step explanation of how a stolen car gets a new identity.
weaknesses: Title and thumbnail overreach the narrow case study.
Phone statistics do not match the Met totals and the Europe share is unlocated.
Editorial prescriptions presented as conclusions; no channel CTA; stale "last year".
Causal and comparative claims (UAE flooding to UK SUV thefts, Georgia sanctions re-exports, "Britain truly does lead") are asserted without sources.
contradictions: "Endless crime destroying Britain" versus a content scope of vehicle and phone theft for export.
"April last year" versus a 2026 publication date.
improvement_opportunities: Retitle to the evidence ("How Stolen UK Cars and Phones Are Shipped Abroad") and align the thumbnail with a container-ship image.
Show on-screen sources (Thatcham/NaVCIS, Met Police) and correct the phone figure to about 81,000.
Replace "last year" with the year and add a closing next-video pointer.
Separate the evidence section from the policy opinion with a spoken label.
unavailable: Primary sources for Border Force, unsolved-theft and Europe phone-theft shares
